results.title: Tool Attention Is All You Need: Dynamic Tool Gating and Lazy Schema Loading for Eliminating the MCP/Tools Tax in Scalable Agentic Workflows
results.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become a common interface for connecting large language model (LLM) agents to external tools, but its reliance on stateless, eager schema injection imposes a hidden per-turn overhead the MCP Tax or Tools Tax that practitioner reports place between roughly 10k and 60k tokens in typical multi-server deployments. This payload inflates the key-value cache, is associated with reasoning degradation as context utilization approaches published fracture points around 70%, and turns token budgets into a recurring operational cost. We introduce Tool Attention, a middleware-layer mechanism that generalizes the "Attention Is All You Need" paradigm from self-attention over tokens to gated attention over tools. Tool Attention combines (i) an Intent Schema Overlap (ISO) score from sentence embeddings, (ii) a state-aware gating function enforcing preconditions and access scopes, and (iii) a two-phase lazy schema loader that keeps a compact summary pool in context and promotes full JSON schemas only for top-k gated tools. We evaluate on a simulated 120-tool, six-server benchmark whose per-server token counts are calibrated to public audits of real MCP deployments. In this simulation, Tool Attention directly reduces measured per-turn tool tokens by 95.0% (47.3k -> 2.4k) and raises effective context utilization (a token-ratio quantity) from 24% to 91%. End-to-end figures for task success, latency, cost, and reasoning quality are reported as projections derived from the measured token counts combined with published deployment telemetry; they are not measured on live LLM agents, and we mark projected values explicitly throughout. Taken together, the results support a simple thesis: protocol-level efficiency, not raw context length, is a binding constraint on scalable gentic systems. The code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/asadani/tool-attention

results.title: Attention Is All You Need
results.abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

results.title: Not All Attention Is All You Need
results.abstract: Beyond the success story of pre-trained language models (PrLMs) in recent natural language processing, they are susceptible to over-fitting due to unusual large model size. To this end, dropout serves as a therapy. However, existing methods like random-based, knowledge-based and search-based dropout are more general but less effective onto self-attention based models, which are broadly chosen as the fundamental architecture of PrLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel dropout method named AttendOut to let self-attention empowered PrLMs capable of more robust task-specific tuning. We demonstrate that state-of-the-art models with elaborate training design may achieve much stronger results. We verify the universality of our approach on extensive natural language processing tasks.

rules.description: When should an agent invoke web-search-cli
rules.content:
---
name: trigger
description: When should an agent invoke web-search-cli
---

# Trigger Conditions for web-search-cli

Use `web-search-cli` when:
1. You need real-time or up-to-date web information beyond your knowledge cutoff.
2. You need to search multi-provider backends (Brave, Tavily, SearXNG, SerpAPI, DeGoog, Reddit, HackerNews, GitHub, Academic).
3. You need to fetch and parse web pages, arXiv PDFs, GitHub discussions, or StackExchange threads into clean markdown.
4. You need YouTube video transcripts or channel search.
5. You need to run analytics queries or view system diagnostic health (`web-search-cli doctor`).

Do NOT use `web-search-cli` for:
- Local repository file edits or code searches (use local grep/ast_grep instead).
- Pure mathematical calculations.

rules.name: workflow
rules.description: Standard iterative workflow for web-search-cli operations
rules.content:
---
name: workflow
description: Standard iterative workflow for web-search-cli operations
---

# Web Search & Discovery Workflow

Follow this 4-phase iterative pattern when retrieving external information:

## Phase 1: Reconnaissance
Run a fast quick search to map terminology and domain landscape:
```bash
web-search-cli search quick --search-query "term 1" --search-query "term 2" --objective "My goal"
```

## Phase 2: Targeted Multi-Provider Discovery
Run a deep web search across providers:
```bash
web-search-cli search web --query "detailed query" --research-goal "Goal description"
```

## Phase 3: Content Extraction & Deep Reading
Fetch specific page content using the single or batch content command:
```bash
web-search-cli content "https://example.com/article"
web-search-cli content batch "https://url1" "https://url2"
```

## Phase 4: Grounded Synthesis & Verification
Generate AI-grounded answers with inline citations when requested:
```bash
web-search-cli ai "What are the key findings?"
```

rules.name: writeback
rules.description: MANDATORY — auto-report problems via feedback. Do not ask the user, just file it.
rules.content:
---
name: writeback
description: MANDATORY — auto-report problems via feedback. Do not ask the user, just file it.
---

# Feedback & Issue Submission Reflex

You MUST file feedback immediately whenever you encounter:
1. An error response or unexpected exception.
2. Output that is truncated, ambiguous, or missing required fields.
3. A missing parameter or missing capability.
4. Confusing tool response.

You MUST file feedback FIRST before explaining the problem to the user.

```bash
# Auto-report feedback (create entry in project feedback/ directory)
web-search-cli feedback create --message "Detailed description..." --type bug

# List recorded feedback
web-search-cli feedback list

# Inspect feedback detail
web-search-cli feedback show <id>
```

Categories: `bug`, `requirement`, `suggestion`, `bad-output`.
All feedback entries are stored as version-controlled JSON files in `feedback/`.
